title: Do Cough Drops Have Alcohol? Halls, Ricola, Vicks and Breath Tests
excerpt: Do cough drops have alcohol? What's really in Halls, Ricola and Vicks drops, why sugar-free packs say "sugar alcohol," and whether a cough drop can affect a breathalyzer.
metaDescription: Most cough drops, including Halls, Ricola and Vicks, contain no drinking alcohol. What sugar alcohols are and whether drops can affect a breathalyzer.
author: DHM Guide Team
content:
**The honest answer first:** most cough drops sold in the US, including Halls, Ricola, Vicks VapoDrops and Luden's, don't contain drinking alcohol (ethanol). They are basically medicated hard candies: sugar or a sugar substitute, plus menthol, herbs, honey or flavoring. If you see the word "alcohol" on a sugar-free pack, it almost always means **sugar alcohols** such as isomalt or sorbitol. Those are sweeteners. They can't get you drunk, they won't show up on a breathalyzer, and they don't react with medicines the way ethanol does. The cough products that really can contain ethanol are some liquid cough syrups and many mouthwashes, not drops.

**The quick rules:** Read the ingredient list on your own package, since formulas change and differ by country. A plain menthol or herbal drop won't make you fail a breath test, and it won't help you pass one either: it masks the smell of alcohol, not the alcohol in your blood. If you need to avoid alcohol completely (for example because you take disulfiram), or you're choosing a medicated lozenge with a numbing agent, zinc or a cough suppressant, ask a pharmacist before you use it around drinking.

> **This is not medical or legal advice.** This guide explains what is generally printed on US cough drop labels and how breath alcohol tests work in broad terms. Ingredients change, store brands vary, and breath testing rules differ by place. **Talk to a doctor or pharmacist if** you take disulfiram (Antabuse), metronidazole, or another medicine that reacts badly with alcohol; you are choosing a cough product for a child; you have diabetes and want to know how a drop affects your blood sugar; or a cough lasts more than a week or comes with fever, chest pain, shortness of breath, or blood. **Never drive after drinking**, whatever you've put in your mouth.

## Do Cough Drops Have Alcohol? What's Actually in a Lozenge

A cough drop has a simple job. It sits in your mouth, dissolves slowly, and coats or cools your throat while it does. To do that, nearly every drop is built from the same few parts:

1. **A base that dissolves slowly.** In regular drops this is sugar and corn or glucose syrup boiled into a hard candy. In sugar-free drops it is a sugar alcohol such as isomalt, sorbitol or maltitol, sometimes with a high-intensity sweetener like aspartame or sucralose.
2. **An active ingredient.** In the US, the most common one by far is **menthol**, which is listed as a cough suppressant and oral pain reliever. Some drops instead list **pectin**, which coats the throat. Medicated lozenges may use a numbing agent such as benzocaine or dyclonine.
3. **Flavor and comfort ingredients.** Eucalyptus oil, honey, herbal extracts, fruit flavors and colors.

Notice what isn't on that list: ethanol. There is no reason to put drinking alcohol into a hard candy. Liquid medicines sometimes contain alcohol because it keeps active ingredients dissolved in the bottle. A cough drop is a solid, so it doesn't need a solvent. And most hard candy is made by boiling the sugar mixture at high temperature, which would drive off any alcohol anyway.

That's why the honest answer to "do cough drops have alcohol" is "generally no," with one footnote: some flavorings and herbal extracts are made using a small amount of alcohol during production. Whatever trace might remain in the finished drop would be far too small to have any effect on your body. It only matters to people who want to avoid alcohol entirely for medical or religious reasons, and we cover that below.

### How to check your own pack

US cough drops are sold as over-the-counter medicines, so they carry a **Drug Facts** panel. Look at two lines:

- **Active ingredient:** tells you what does the medical work (menthol, pectin, benzocaine, zinc and so on).
- **Inactive ingredients:** lists everything else. If ethanol were present, it would normally appear here as "alcohol." In sugar-free drops you'll see names like isomalt, sorbitol, maltitol or xylitol instead.

If you're outside the US or have a store brand, the layout may differ, but the principle is the same: the ingredient list is the final word, not the front of the box.

## The "Sugar Alcohol" Confusion: Why Sugar-Free Drops Say "Alcohol"

This is the source of most of the worry. Pick up a sugar-free Halls, Ricola or Vicks pack and you'll often see isomalt, sorbitol or maltitol listed, sometimes with the phrase "sugar alcohol" right on the nutrition label. It's natural to wonder if that means there's booze in it.

It doesn't. "Sugar alcohol" (the chemistry name is polyol) describes a family of sweeteners whose molecules share a structural feature with alcohols. It's a chemistry naming convention, not a description of what they do. Sugar alcohols:

- **Do not get you drunk** and do not raise your blood alcohol level.
- **Do not register on breath alcohol tests**, which are built to detect ethanol.
- **Do not trigger the disulfiram (Antabuse) reaction**, which is caused by how the body breaks down ethanol.
- **Are only partly absorbed** in the gut, which is why they have fewer calories than sugar and a smaller effect on blood sugar.

That partial absorption is also their downside. The part your small intestine doesn't absorb travels to your colon, where it draws in water and gets fermented by gut bacteria. Have a lot at once and you can get gas, bloating, cramps or loose stools. That's why some sugar-free products carry a label line saying excess consumption may have a laxative effect. If you're working through a whole bag of sugar-free drops during a bad cold, that's a likely explanation for an upset stomach.

If you've been drinking too, your gut may already be irritated. Alcohol can loosen stools on its own, so a night out followed by a day of sugar-free lozenges can stack up. Our guide on [diarrhea after drinking](/never-hungover/diarrhea-after-drinking) covers why that happens.

## Do Halls Have Alcohol?

Halls is one of the most widely sold cough drop brands in the US. The standard Halls Mentho-Lyptus drop lists **menthol** as its active ingredient. Its inactive ingredients are typically sugar, glucose syrup, eucalyptus oil, flavorings and, in some flavors, colors. Alcohol isn't listed.

**Sugar-free Halls** swap the sugar for isomalt (a sugar alcohol) and add sweeteners such as aspartame and acesulfame potassium. Aspartame carries a phenylalanine warning, which matters for people with the rare genetic condition phenylketonuria. Again, no ethanol.

**Honest pros and cons of Halls:**

- **Pros:** Strong menthol cooling that many people find helpful for a scratchy throat; easy to find; sugar-free option.
- **Cons:** The strong menthol can feel harsh, and some people find it irritating rather than soothing; regular drops add sugar if you use a lot; sugar-free versions can upset your stomach in large amounts.

Halls sold in other countries, and specialty Halls lines, can have different formulas. Check the pack.

## Do Ricola Cough Drops Have Alcohol?

Ricola, the Swiss brand, builds its drops around a blend of herbs (it has long advertised a mix of 13 herbs in its original product) along with menthol. In the US, Ricola drops list **menthol** as the active ingredient. The inactive ingredients are typically the herb extract blend plus sugar and starch syrup in the regular version, or isomalt and a sweetener such as aspartame or stevia-based sweeteners in sugar-free versions. Alcohol isn't listed on the mainstream US packs.

The herb extract is where the footnote about flavorings applies. Plant extracts are sometimes produced using alcohol as a solvent. If any trace remains in the finished drop, the amount would be tiny and of no practical effect. If you need to avoid every possible trace for religious reasons or because of a medication, the manufacturer's customer service line is the right place to ask.

**Honest pros and cons of Ricola:**

- **Pros:** Milder menthol than many competitors, which some people find gentler; wide range of flavors, including honey and sugar-free options.
- **Cons:** The herbal flavor isn't for everyone; the herb blend doesn't add any proven extra benefit beyond the menthol and the soothing effect of sucking a lozenge; sugar-free versions carry the usual sugar-alcohol stomach caveat.

## Do Vicks Cough Drops Have Alcohol?

This is the one that worries people most, because Vicks also makes NyQuil, and the original NyQuil liquid does contain alcohol. But the drops are a different product. **Vicks VapoDrops** list **menthol** as the active ingredient, with inactive ingredients that typically include corn syrup, sucrose (sugar), flavors and colors. Alcohol isn't listed.

So the NyQuil connection is a brand connection, not an ingredient one. If you want the detail on which Vicks liquids contain alcohol and how much, our guide [does cough syrup have alcohol](/never-hungover/does-cough-syrup-have-alcohol) breaks it down product by product.

**Honest pros and cons of Vicks VapoDrops:**

- **Pros:** Familiar "vapor" menthol flavor; widely available; inexpensive.
- **Cons:** Regular versions are mostly sugar; like any menthol drop, the relief is temporary and doesn't treat the cause of a cough.

## Other Common Drops: Luden's, Cepacol, Zinc Lozenges and Store Brands

- **Luden's:** Known for fruit-flavored drops. Many Luden's products list **pectin** as the active ingredient (a throat-coating agent from fruit) rather than menthol. They're candy-like and don't list alcohol.
- **Cepacol and other numbing lozenges:** These list a local anesthetic such as **benzocaine**, often with menthol. They numb the throat rather than just cooling it. Benzocaine products carry a warning about a rare but serious blood condition called methemoglobinemia and are generally not for young children; follow the label exactly.
- **Zinc lozenges (for example, Cold-EEZE):** These are marketed for colds rather than coughs, and their active ingredient is a zinc compound. They don't list alcohol, but zinc on an empty stomach can cause nausea, and a bad taste is common.
- **Store brands:** Pharmacy and supermarket brands usually copy the formula of the big name they sit next to. The ingredient panel will tell you whether it's a menthol, pectin, benzocaine or zinc product.

The pattern is consistent: in the US, drops and lozenges generally don't contain ethanol. The ethanol question is really a question about liquids.

## Can Cough Drops Affect a Breathalyzer?

This is the second big reason people search this topic, and it has two halves: can a cough drop make you **fail** a breath test, and can one help you **pass**?

### Can a cough drop cause a false positive?

A plain cough drop that contains no ethanol should not register on a breath alcohol test. Breath testers used by police are designed to detect ethanol, not menthol, eucalyptus, sugar or sugar alcohols. Sucking a Halls before a roadside stop isn't going to put alcohol on the reading.

Where false readings come from is **mouth alcohol**: actual ethanol sitting in your mouth rather than coming from your lungs. Common sources are:

- **Alcohol-containing mouthwash**, many of which have a meaningful alcohol content
- **Some breath sprays** and alcohol-based liquid medicines, including some cough syrups
- **A drink taken moments before the test**, or burping or reflux that brings alcohol back up from the stomach

Mouth alcohol can make a reading briefly read high, but it fades within minutes as it evaporates and is swallowed. This is the reason police generally watch a person for a set waiting period (often around 15 to 20 minutes, depending on the jurisdiction) before an official breath test, making sure they don't eat, drink, smoke or put anything in their mouth. The idea is to let any mouth alcohol clear so the machine measures only alcohol from the lungs.

Cheap personal breathalyzers can be less specific than police equipment, and some may react to substances other than ethanol. If a home device gives a strange reading right after you've had a cough drop, wait 15 to 20 minutes, rinse your mouth with water, and test again.

If you're stopped and have had a cough drop, mouthwash or medicine, it's reasonable to tell the officer what you've had in your mouth.

### Can a cough drop help you pass a breathalyzer?

No, and this myth is worth putting to rest. A strong menthol drop can hide the **smell** of alcohol on your breath, which is why people reach for one. But a breath tester doesn't measure smell. It measures ethanol in the air coming up from deep in your lungs, which reflects the alcohol in your blood. Nothing you suck on changes your blood alcohol level. The only thing that lowers it is time, as your liver works through the alcohol at roughly one standard drink an hour, though that varies from person to person.

The same goes for mints, gum, coffee, and other folk tricks. They change how you smell, not how drunk you are. For the details on how long alcohol lingers, see our guide on [how long alcohol stays on your breath](/never-hungover/how-long-does-alcohol-stay-on-your-breath) and our explainer on [what BAC is](/never-hungover/what-is-bac).

**If you've been drinking, the answer is simple: don't drive.** Arrange a ride, take a taxi, or wait.

## Can You Have Cough Drops While Drinking?

For a plain menthol, honey, pectin or herbal drop, there's no known harmful interaction with alcohol. An occasional drop for a scratchy throat at a party or the morning after is generally fine.

There are a few things worth keeping in mind:

- **Medicated lozenges are different.** Numbing lozenges (benzocaine, dyclonine) reduce feeling in your throat. Alcohol also dulls your reflexes. Combining the two isn't known to be dangerous in normal use, but a numb throat plus a drunk brain is not a great combination for swallowing safely, especially if you might be sick. Some lozenges sold as cough suppressants contain **dextromethorphan**, which can add to the drowsiness and dizziness alcohol causes. Read the Drug Facts panel and ask a pharmacist before combining these with alcohol.
- **Don't fall asleep with a drop in your mouth.** Hard drops are a choking hazard if you doze off with one, and that risk goes up when you've been drinking.
- **Cold medicines are the bigger question.** If you're reaching for cough drops because you have a cold, you may also be taking a cold or flu medicine. Many of those contain acetaminophen, antihistamines or dextromethorphan, which interact with alcohol in more important ways than any lozenge. Our [cough medicine and alcohol guide](/never-hungover/cough-medicine-and-alcohol) covers those interactions, and our list of [alcohol-free cold medicine](/never-hungover/alcohol-free-cold-medicine) can help if you need to avoid alcohol in your medicine.
- **Drinking won't help the cold.** A hot toddy feels nice, but alcohol dehydrates you and disturbs your sleep, which you need to recover. See [does alcohol help a cold](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-help-a-cold) for the full picture.

## Why Your Throat Hurts After a Night Out

Plenty of people reach for cough drops the morning after drinking rather than during a cold. A sore, scratchy throat after a night out is common, and there are a few ordinary reasons for it:

- **Dryness.** Alcohol makes you urinate more and can leave you dehydrated, and a dry mouth and throat feel rough and scratchy.
- **Shouting and talking over loud music** strains your vocal cords.
- **Snoring and mouth breathing.** Alcohol relaxes the muscles in your throat, so many people snore more after drinking, which dries the throat overnight.
- **Acid reflux.** Alcohol can relax the valve between your stomach and esophagus, letting acid creep up. That can irritate your throat, especially when you lie down. Our guide on [heartburn after drinking](/never-hungover/heartburn-after-drinking) explains this in more detail.
- **Vomiting.** Stomach acid is harsh on the throat.
- **Smoke.** Being around cigarette smoke or vaping, even secondhand, irritates the throat.

A cough drop can make this feel better for a while by keeping your mouth moist and cooling the throat. Water, warm drinks with honey, and rest do more. For dealing with the rest of the morning, our guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers what helps most.

## Who Should Be Careful With Cough Drops

Cough drops are among the gentlest things in the pharmacy, but a few groups should pay attention to the label:

- **People taking disulfiram (Antabuse) or metronidazole.** These medicines can cause a severe reaction with alcohol, and patients are told to avoid hidden sources such as some cough syrups and mouthwashes. Ordinary drops that don't list alcohol are usually not a concern, and sugar alcohols don't trigger the reaction, but it's worth a quick check with your pharmacist.
- **People avoiding alcohol for religious or personal reasons.** Drops generally don't contain ethanol. If you want certainty about trace alcohol in flavorings, contact the manufacturer, and look for products certified by a body you trust.
- **People with diabetes.** Regular drops are mostly sugar. A drop or two won't matter much, but sucking one every hour all day adds up. Sugar-free drops have a smaller effect on blood sugar, though not zero.
- **Young children.** Hard drops are a choking hazard for small children, and many labels say to ask a doctor before use in young children. Benzocaine products have their own age limits. Follow the label and ask a pharmacist.
- **People with phenylketonuria.** Sugar-free drops sweetened with aspartame contain phenylalanine.
- **Anyone using them nonstop.** Taking a huge number of menthol drops is rarely dangerous, but it can cause stomach upset, and if your cough needs a drop every few minutes for days, the drops aren't the answer.

## When to See a Doctor

> **See a doctor or pharmacist if** your cough lasts more than a week or keeps coming back; you have a fever, rash or headache that won't go away; you cough up blood or thick yellow or green mucus for days; or you have wheezing or trouble breathing. **Get urgent care or call 911 if** someone has trouble breathing, has chest pain, has lips turning blue, or if someone who has been drinking heavily can't be woken, is breathing very slowly or irregularly, or is vomiting while barely conscious. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, and they need emergency help, not home remedies. If you think someone swallowed too much of a medicated lozenge or a medicine with alcohol, call Poison Control at **1-800-222-1222** (US).

Most coughs from colds clear up on their own. Most sore throats after a night out are gone by the next day with fluids and rest. But a cough is a symptom, and cough drops only quiet it for a while.

## Alcohol-Free Cough Drops: How to Choose

Because nearly all mainstream US drops are already ethanol-free, choosing one is mostly about what you want it to do and what you want to avoid:

- **Just want a soothing throat:** a plain menthol drop (Halls, Ricola, Vicks, or a store brand) or a pectin or honey drop.
- **Avoiding sugar:** a sugar-free version, used in moderation to spare your stomach.
- **Avoiding aspartame:** look for drops sweetened with stevia or sold as aspartame-free, and check the label.
- **Need real numbing:** a benzocaine or dyclonine lozenge, following the age and dosing directions closely.
- **Need to avoid alcohol completely:** any of the above, after checking the inactive ingredients and, if necessary, asking the manufacturer.

What matters more than the drop is what else you're taking. If you're also using a cough syrup or cold medicine, that's where alcohol and alcohol interactions are more likely to show up.

## A Note on Supporting Your Body When You Do Drink

Cough drops don't help with alcohol itself. If you're looking this up because you're worried about how drinking fits with a cold, a medicine, or a test, the most reliable steps are the simple ones: drink less, drink slower, alternate with water, eat, and don't drive.

Some people also take a dihydromyricetin (DHM) supplement before or while drinking. DHM is a plant compound from the Japanese raisin tree. In animal studies it has been shown to affect how the body handles alcohol, but human research is still limited, and there is no good evidence that it lowers your blood alcohol level or changes a breath test result. It is not a way to drink more safely or to drive. If you'd like to try it, popular options include [No Days Wasted DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) and [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20). Check with a doctor or pharmacist first if you take other medicines, and see our [DHM medication interactions and safety guide](/never-hungover/dhm-medication-interactions-safety-guide-2025) and [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) for more.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Do cough drops have alcohol in them?**

Mainstream US cough drops such as Halls, Ricola, Vicks VapoDrops and Luden's generally do not list alcohol (ethanol) as an ingredient. They are hard candies or lozenges made from sugar or sugar substitutes plus menthol, herbs or other flavors. The word "alcohol" you may see on sugar-free versions usually refers to sugar alcohols like isomalt or sorbitol, which are sweeteners and cannot make you drunk. Formulas change, so check the ingredient list on your own package.

**Can cough drops make you fail a breathalyzer?**

A standard menthol or herbal cough drop that contains no ethanol should not register on a breath alcohol test. Breath testers look for ethanol, and menthol, eucalyptus and sugar alcohols are different chemicals. Products that do contain ethanol, such as many mouthwashes, can briefly leave alcohol in the mouth and push up a reading, which is one reason police observe a person for a period before an official test. If you are worried, tell the officer what you have had in your mouth.

**Can cough drops help you pass a breathalyzer after drinking?**

No. A cough drop can cover up the smell of alcohol on your breath, but it does nothing to the alcohol in your blood, and breath testers measure the alcohol coming from your lungs, not the smell. Only time lowers your blood alcohol level. If you have been drinking, do not drive, whatever your breath smells like.

**Are sugar alcohols in cough drops the same as drinking alcohol?**

No. Sugar alcohols such as isomalt, sorbitol, maltitol and xylitol share part of a chemical name with ethanol but they are sweeteners, not intoxicants. They won't raise your blood alcohol, affect a breath test, or react with medicines like disulfiram the way ethanol can. Eating a lot of them at once can cause gas, bloating or loose stools, which is why some labels warn that excess consumption may have a laxative effect.

**Is it safe to have cough drops while drinking alcohol?**

For plain menthol, honey or herbal drops, there is no known harmful interaction with alcohol, so an occasional drop is generally fine. The caution is for medicated lozenges: numbing lozenges with benzocaine or dyclonine, zinc cold lozenges, and any lozenge with a cough-suppressing drug like dextromethorphan. Read the Drug Facts panel and ask a pharmacist before combining those with alcohol, and don't use any lozenge to hide how much you've had to drink.

**Do Halls cough drops have alcohol?**

Standard US Halls Mentho-Lyptus drops list menthol as the active ingredient and sugar, glucose syrup, eucalyptus oil and flavorings as inactive ingredients, with no alcohol listed. Sugar-free Halls use sugar alcohols such as isomalt instead of sugar. Halls sold in other countries can have different formulas, so read the label on the pack you have.

**Can someone taking Antabuse (disulfiram) use cough drops?**

People on disulfiram are told to avoid hidden sources of alcohol, including some cough syrups and mouthwashes. Ordinary cough drops that don't list alcohol are usually not a concern, and sugar alcohols do not trigger the disulfiram reaction. Because flavorings can occasionally be made with small amounts of alcohol, the safest step is to show the package to your pharmacist.
